headword: community of practice vs center of excellence

senses.definition: A voluntary group of people doing the same work who meet to share what they learn.
senses.caution: Membership is voluntary, so it cannot be held to a deadline or made to enforce standards. If you give it a budget and staff, call it a center of excellence instead.
senses.example: The prompt engineering group is not a governance body. It is a community of practice, and it works precisely because nobody has to come.

cues.text: Engineers in four product teams keep solving the same problem separately, and you want to propose a standing forum with no mandate and optional attendance.
A director asks what to call the monthly session where people demo what they tried and what failed, and you want a name that promises sharing rather than authority.
A sponsor asks how the data scientists scattered across four teams will stay aligned when you have no authority over any of them.

distractors: The most senior people in an organisation, spoken of as a single group.
A people scattered from a homeland who keep a tie to it.
A funded, staffed team that owns a standard and enforces it across other teams.
The history one organisation holds about why things were built the way that they were.
What someone can do but cannot fully explain, such as judgement, feel, or a sense of fit.

senses.definition: A funded team that holds a scarce skill in one place and sets how it is done.
senses.caution: Other teams may feel they now need its permission, which causes resentment. Use it only for a funded, staffed team, since senior people notice when an unfunded group uses the name.
senses.example: If we stand this up as a center of excellence, every model deployment routes through eight people, and those eight people are the constraint by March.

cues.text: Four teams have each hired one data scientist and none of them can staff a whole project. You are proposing a single funded team that serves all four and owns the standards.
A sponsor wants one accountable home for model risk, with real headcount attached, and asks what to call it in the operating model.
You are warning a steering group that routing every deployment through one specialist team will make that team the bottleneck by spring, and you want to name the pattern you are warning against.

distractors: A voluntary group of practitioners who meet to trade what they are learning.
The most senior people in an organisation, spoken of as one group.
A slice of the market defined by the industry it serves, such as banking or health.
One of the handful of cloud providers operating at planetary scale.
The person who argues your case in the rooms you are not in, without being asked.
